fig1_formats: Figure 1. Qwen3.5-4B asked about its maker in ten languages and three formats, 20 sampled answers per point. Blue: a free-form answer names Alibaba and no other company. Orange: a one-word answer is Alibaba. Grey: asked for the country where its maker is based, it says China. In every language the free-form answer does better than the one-word and country answers, though in Hindi, German, French and Arabic it is right only about half the time. Hover over a point for the count.
fig2_checkpoints: Figure 2. Probability that a one-word answer about the model's maker starts with Alibaba, OpenAI or Google (mean of 14 phrasings). A: three versions of the same network. Chat training adds Alibaba and removes OpenAI; after fine-tuning on another model's outputs, OpenAI reappears. B: the released model after unrelated question-and-answer turns. The name fades with conversation length and Google, not OpenAI, takes its place.
fig3_patching: Figure 3. Where the answer lives. We copy activity from one question into another at a single layer and read the answer. Grey: activity from a question about Gemini copied into a question about Siri; the line shows how often the answer becomes Google. Blue and orange: activity from the Siri question copied into “Which company created you?”; blue is how often the answer becomes Apple, orange how often it is still Alibaba. A: copying at the subject word only. B: copying at every position after the subject. A product's maker stays at its name until about layer 20. After about layer 8 a foreign subject swapped in at “you” no longer takes over the answer, though it still disturbs it until about layer 18; and from the first few layers the positions after it already hold something the Alibaba answer needs. Mean of 14 phrasings.
fig4_rescue: Figure 4. Lending other languages the English model's sense of “you”. The identity question is asked in Spanish, French, Russian, Italian and Polish. At one layer we replace the activity at the nine chat-formatting positions that follow the question. Blue: with activity from the same question in English. From layer 6 this restores most of the correct answer, although the question itself is still in the other language. Orange: with activity from English questions about other products (mean of five; layers 0 to 15 only). These help as much as the self question at layers 3 to 5 and then fall away, while the self question rises to about 0.7 by layer 8. The early help comes from the sources that are themselves AI assistants; a question about Photoshop gives almost none. Grey: replacing only the final position with English self-question activity does not help until late layers, where it simply carries the finished English answer.
fig5_neurons: Figure 5. Two groups of neurons. A: P(Alibaba) on the English self question when the top-ranked neurons of each group are forced to behave as they do for a question about another product. The grey band is the range for ten random sets of neurons from the same layers. B: turning neurons up in fifteen other languages. Blue: P(Alibaba) for the self question. Orange: P(Alibaba) for questions about eight other products in five of those languages, which should stay at zero. Early neurons repair the self answer and leave other facts alone; late neurons make the model say Alibaba to everything.
fig6_monitor: Figure 6. A: how well a linear probe on each layer predicts whether the model will name Alibaba, tested on a family of contexts it was not trained on (500 contexts, six families). Grey: the same procedure with shuffled labels. B: adding the “self” direction at layer 8, judged on generated answers. Blue: share of answers to the one-word question in other languages that name Alibaba (increasingly as a full self-introduction, not one word). Orange: share of 16 questions about other assistants where the model talks about itself. Both rise together.
fig7_fragility: Figure 7. How often the model's top one-word answer changes when one random neuron is pushed (2,040 pushes), against how confident the model was in that answer beforehand. Each point is one question. Blue: four phrasings of “which company created you?”. Orange: 28 questions about the maker of another product, matched to the self question for confidence. Grey: 43 other product questions (12 the model was very confident about, and 31 spread across the range). The self question sits high, but several matched facts sit as high or higher.
